newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spaniards see economic improvement in 1997 - poll.
newsitem.headline: Spaniards see economic improvement in 1997 - poll.

text.p: The Spanish applaud many of the minority Popular Party government's economic policies but are less convinced by some of its political initiatives, a poll published in a Spanish newspaper on Sunday showed.
Of those surveyed, 37.9 percent believed that in 1997 under the conservatives -- who took over the administration last year after 13 years of Socialist rule -- the economic situation would improve.

The government won most support for its pension pact with unions and the decline in interest rates, according to the survey of 1,000 adults by Spanish pollster Sigma Dos between December 24 and January 2 and published in the daily El Mundo.

According to the poll, 30.1 percent saw the drop in the official interest rate to 6.25 percent from nine percent, and the resulting decline in mortgage and other rates, as last year's most important event.
Of those surveyed, 42.9 percent supported the government's pension pact to secure payments in the 1997 budget and beyond.
A sizeable majority of those polled also backed the government's cut in taxes to small businesses, the rise in alcohol and tobacco taxes and the liberalisation steps in the communications sector.

But many did not support the government's tougher stance towards Cuba's government, with 46.8 percent against the policy that prompted a diplomatic row late last year as an angry Cuba ejected Spain's ambassador.

Many also took a dim view of the government's decision -- against its own campaign pledge -- not to publish the CESID spy documents that could link former government officials to the "dirty war" against Basque guerrillas in the 1980s.
